title: MLOps, deployment & observability
summary: Make a model a maintainable service with measurable behavior and a rollback path.
html:
Make a model a maintainable service with measurable behavior and a rollback path.

Version the complete release

A model artifact is one component. Record weights, tokenizer, preprocessing, prompts, retrieval index, runtime version, and configuration. Releasing a new embedding model without rebuilding a compatible index can break retrieval even when both components work independently.

Define service objectives

Choose meaningful targets for availability, latency, quality, and cost. Measure first-token and full-response time separately for streaming generation. Track queue time, model execution, retrieval, and tool calls so bottlenecks are attributable. Sample traces carefully to avoid collecting unnecessary sensitive content.

Stage the rollout

Use offline evaluation, shadow traffic, canary deployment, and controlled experiments where suitable. A rollback must restore compatible artifacts and configuration. Health checks should exercise a real inference path without treating a successful response as proof of semantic quality.

Monitor changing behavior

Input drift describes changing inputs; concept drift describes a changing relationship between inputs and targets. Delayed labels complicate monitoring. Establish feedback collection, incident ownership, and scheduled evaluation. Alert on user-impacting failures rather than every harmless statistical movement.

Worked example

A retrieval service’s latency doubles after a release. A trace shows model inference unchanged but index search increased from 30 ms to 400 ms. Rolling back the model alone does nothing; the index configuration and query pipeline are part of the release.

What goes wrong

A model loading successfully is not an end-to-end deployment test. A public endpoint must be tested through the same route and authentication boundaries users encounter.

Check your understanding

What makes a model rollback incomplete?

Reveal the explanation

Restoring weights while leaving incompatible prompts, preprocessing, tokenizer, or retrieval index can preserve the failure or create a different one.

How the pieces connect

A usable chapter has a flow of decisions, evidence, and checks. Use this diagram as a navigation aid, then test each step on a small real example.

An operating model for mlops, deployment & observability

A deployment is a configuration of interacting artifacts, not a model file. Tokenizers, feature pipelines, vector indexes, prompts, model weights, tool permissions, and runtime versions can all change behavior. Treat the full configuration as a versioned release unit.

The diagram is deliberately sequential, but real systems loop. A surprising result may expose a bad representation; a production incident may reveal a missing evaluation slice; a performance limit may require an algorithmic change. The point is to preserve the link between the abstract concept, the evidence you observe, and the decision you make next.

Worked system: a rollback that restores the wrong system

A release changes an embedding model but leaves the old vector index in place. The service remains available, requests return answers, and a generic health check passes—yet retrieval quality collapses because query and document vectors now live in incompatible spaces. Rolling back only the model weights may not fix it if the index, tokenizer, prompt, feature definitions, or configuration changed with the release.

Version the release as a set of compatible artifacts. A canary should exercise the same authorization, retrieval, inference, and monitoring path as a user. Define rollback before rollout, then rehearse it with a representative request. Availability is necessary; semantic behavior, cost, and evidence quality need their own signals.

Notebook: Instrument one request end to end

Use this as an inspection pattern, not a drop-in production implementation. The specific values will change, but the habit remains: expose the assumption, calculate the boundary, and preserve the evidence that supports the next decision.

trace = {"queue_ms": queue, "retrieve_ms": retrieve,
         "prefill_ms": prefill, "decode_ms": decode}
assert sum(trace.values()) <= latency_slo_ms
# Attribute latency before changing infrastructure.
What to test next. 1. Package: Version model, data transforms, prompts, index, and runtime. 2. Release: Shadow, canary, or gate a controlled cohort. 3. Observe: Trace quality, latency, cost, drift, and failures. 4. Recover: Roll back compatible artifacts and investigate.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Package. Version model, data transforms, prompts, index, and runtime.
  2. Release. Shadow, canary, or gate a controlled cohort.
  3. Observe. Trace quality, latency, cost, drift, and failures.
  4. Recover. Roll back compatible artifacts and investigate.

Make rollback a rehearsed operation. Confirm that a candidate release can serve a real representative request through the same route, authorization, and monitoring path as a user.

Questions that keep the chapter honest

AskWhy it mattersEvidence to collect
What assumptions does this method make?Every method encodes a view of data, hardware, or behavior.Inputs, representations, constraints, and cases outside the expected range.
What would make the result fail?Failure modes show where an aggregate result is fragile.Boundary cases, counterexamples, slices, and perturbations.
What decision changes if it improves?A metric only matters through an operational action.Baseline, threshold, cost, latency, and human-review consequences.
